questions.q: Why does ServiceNow use a two-stage Import Set pattern instead of writing external data directly into a target table?
options: So that a bad or malformed row in the source data never corrupts a live, production-facing table
Because target tables cannot accept more than one new record per day
Because Transform Maps are required before any table can store data at all
Because staging tables are faster to query than target tables
questions.explain: Staging isolates raw, unvalidated data so problems are caught and fixed before anything reaches a real table.

questions.q: What does the auto-created Import Set staging table actually contain right after a load?
options: A raw, unmodified copy of the source rows, with columns matching the source file or feed exactly
A fully validated and mapped copy of the data, ready for production use
Only the rows that failed validation against the target table
A summary count of how many rows were loaded, with no actual row data
questions.explain: The staging table is a literal landing zone — nothing is cleaned, validated, or mapped at this stage.

questions.q: What naming convention does ServiceNow use for auto-created Import Set staging tables?
options: They're prefixed with `imp_`, such as `imp_new_employees`
They're always named exactly `staging_table`
They reuse the exact name of the target table
They're prefixed with `sys_` like core system tables
questions.explain: ServiceNow prefixes auto-created staging tables with `imp_`, inferring the schema from the source data's own columns.

questions.q: In the full import pipeline, what is the correct order of responsibility?
options: A Data Source populates the Import Set staging table, then a Transform Map moves that staged data into the target table
A Transform Map populates the staging table, then a Data Source maps it to the target table
The target table is populated first, then a Data Source archives it into a staging table
Data Sources and Transform Maps both write directly to the target table independently
questions.explain: Data Sources fill the staging table (Lesson 25); Transform Maps then empty it into a real target table (Lesson 26).

questions.q: If one row in a source CSV has a malformed email address, what happens under ServiceNow's Import Set pattern?
options: That row lands in the staging table as-is and can be inspected and fixed there, without corrupting the target table
The entire import silently fails with no record of any row
The malformed row is automatically deleted and never appears anywhere
The target table accepts the malformed value without any way to catch it
questions.explain: Because staging is separate from transforming, a bad row stays visible and fixable in the staging table instead of reaching production data.
